title: Exponential Advantage of Quantum over Classical References in Leakage Detection
abstract: Leakage from a known encoding subspace can be detected by projection. However, the corresponding projector is unavailable when the encoding subspace is not classically specified. Here we show how independent quantum references prepared by the same encoder enable leakage detection without a classical description of the encoding. A coherent measurement on the references and a single message leaves every state within the two-dimensional encoding subspace, including its entanglement with a remote system, exactly unchanged. We derive the exact detection law for $M$ ideal references and prove optimality among tests with zero false alarm for every encoding. For orthogonal leakage, the miss probability is asymptotic to $4/M$, independent of the ambient dimension $d$. Measuring all references first, even collectively, gives zero detection at every finite budget under the same zero-false-alarm requirement. For a fixed detection target between zero and one, the optimal measurement-first cost is $Θ(d/ε)$ at sufficiently small tolerance $ε$ on normal false alarm and conditional disturbance; a dimension-independent coherent budget suffices. For one logical qubit encoded in three physical qubits, seven coherent references achieve at least $50\%$ orthogonal-leakage detection, whereas any measurement-first receiver needs at least $588$ under the same $1\%$ normal tolerances. Quantum references thus support leakage checks without classical reconstruction, with a sample advantage exponential in the number of physical qubits.
summary: This paper introduces a method for detecting quantum leakage from an unknown encoding subspace using multiple independent quantum references measured coherently. It rigorously proves that this quantum approach is exponentially superior to classical measurement-first protocols, especially when the encoding structure is unknown. This advances the understanding of quantum resource utilization in quantum information security and verification.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of detecting quantum leakage from an encoding subspace when the subspace itself is not classically specified.
main_result: A coherent measurement using independent quantum references provides an optimal detection law with a sample advantage exponential in the number of physical qubits compared to measurement-first classical protocols.
method: The authors derive detection laws by comparing the performance of a coherent joint measurement (quantum) against a sequential measurement-first (classical) protocol.
model_or_system: The model involves quantum information processing where a message is encoded into a subspace, and leakage is defined as population outside this subspace. The comparison is made between coherent reference measurements and classical POVM measurements.
key_observables: Detection probability ($D_0$), false alarm rate ($\epsilon$), miss probability, and the required number of quantum references ($M$).
important_parameters: Number of references ($M$), ambient dimension ($d$), and tolerance ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The coherent check is assumed to be optimal among all tests with zero false alarm for every encoding, and the analysis often assumes ideal reference operations or specific noise models (e.g., local Markov Pauli channels).
figures_summary: Figures compare the required number of references ($M$) for quantum vs. measurement-first approaches, demonstrating an exponential advantage for the coherent check, and illustrate the process flow difference between the two detection methods.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the problem of leakage detection without classical knowledge of the subspace. It then derives the optimal detection law for the coherent measurement, contrasts this with the limitations of measurement-first receivers, and quantifies the resulting exponential quantum advantage.
why_interesting: The focus on quantum reference measurements to overcome the need for classical knowledge of the encoding subspace is highly relevant to quantum error correction and quantum communication protocols where full state tomography or classical description is impossible.
